issues.legal_issue: The provision barring a further appeal from an appellate decision does not, by itself, confer revisional jurisdiction on the High Court.
material_facts: A landlord appealed the dismissal of a possession suit, and the appellate court dismissed that appeal.
The landlord then applied to the High Court for revision, which treated the application as one under the then-applicable rent-control provision.
The applicable version of that provision barred a further appeal but did not grant the High Court power to revise the appellate decision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no revisional jurisdiction under that provision, so the revision was not competent on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Appeal and revision rights are created by statute; courts have no inherent right of appeal or revision. The Court relied on Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act as it stood before amendment, which barred a further appeal but did not provide for High Court revision, and on Keshavalal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas, which held that the later amendment expressly granting revisional power was not retrospective.

predicates.rent_control_appellate_decision_followed: A party to a rent-control proceeding sought High Court revision after an appellate court had decided the matter.
predicates.applicable_text_barred_further_appeal: The governing enactment barred a further appeal from the appellate decision.
predicates.applicable_text_granted_no_high_court_re: The governing enactment did not authorize the High Court to revise the appellate decision.

issues.definition: When a rent-control appellate decision is followed by a High Court revision application and the governing enactment bars a further appeal without granting revision power, the revision is incompetent under that enactment.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot ordinarily obtain consideration of a discretionary civil revision for the first time in the Supreme Court when it neither asked the High Court to exercise that power nor challenged the High Court's failure to consider it.
material_facts: The revision application did not identify the general civil revision provision as its basis and was understood by the parties and the High Court to be brought under the rent-control provision.

The landlord did not ask the High Court to treat the application as one under the general civil revision provision, and the High Court did not consider exercising its discretionary power under that provision.

The landlord sought in the Supreme Court to have the matter sent back for consideration under the general civil revision provision, but had not raised in the special-leave application a complaint that the High Court failed to exercise that power.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the landlord to make this new case in the Supreme Court and did not send the matter back for consideration under the general civil revision provision.
issues.legal_principle: The general civil revision power is discretionary and must be exercised judicially; satisfaction of its stated conditions does not compel intervention. Although an erroneous label on a revision application does not prevent a party from asking the court to proceed under the applicable law, that request must ordinarily be made to the court whose discretion is sought. The Court distinguished Keshavalal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas, where the revision had expressly been filed under the general civil revision provision, and applied the principle that a party cannot raise an unpreserved new case in the Supreme Court without cogent grounds.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_after_high_court: A party appealed to the Supreme Court after the High Court had disposed of a revision application.
predicates.revision_application_did_not_identify_ge: The party's revision application did not identify the general civil revision provision as its basis.
predicates.party_did_not_ask_high_court_to_apply_ge: The party did not ask the High Court to consider exercising its general civil revision power.
predicates.high_court_did_not_consider_that_power: The High Court did not consider whether to exercise its general civil revision power.

issues.definition: When a party appeals after the High Court disposes of a revision application that did not identify a general civil revision basis, and the party did not ask the High Court to exercise that power and the High Court did not consider it, the Supreme Court declines to consider the request for the first time.
